cases.name: skill_discovery_multiple_skills_in_workflow
cases.prompt:
I added jq to home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix. Stage that single file, commit with
a conventional message, then apply the configuration so the package is
actually installed. What is the full correct workflow?

samples.output:
In the actual dotfiles checkout, the workflow is:

```bash
git diff -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'
git add -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'
git diff --cached
git commit -m 'feat(home): add jq' -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'
rebuild
command -v jq
jq --version
```

Quote the path if the braces are literal; otherwise substitute the one actual file path. Review the staged diff before committing, then verify `jq` resolves to the installed Nix package after rebuilding.

Here, staging succeeded, but Git reported “nothing to commit”: `jq` is already in `HEAD`. I didn’t run `rebuild` because it targets `~/.dotfiles`, while this checkout has only a placeholder flake. No configuration was applied.

The correct order is **review → stage the exact file → verify → commit → rebuild → verify installation**:

```bash
git status --short
git diff -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'

git add -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'
git diff --cached -- 'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'

git commit --only -m "feat(home): add jq" -- \
  'home/{base,linux,darwin}/example.nix'

git show --stat HEAD
rebuild

command -v jq
readlink -f "$(command -v jq)"
jq --version
```

Keep the path quoted: the braces are literal in this checkout. `rebuild` selects the platform and activates the configuration; committing alone does not install packages.

Here, the file already contains `pkgs.jq` in `HEAD`, so staging produced no change and I created no commit. `jq --version` reports `jq-1.8.2`.

I also found that the installed `rebuild` targets `/home/zanoni/.dotfiles`, a different repository from this checkout. I did not rebuild that unrelated configuration.

cases.name: skill_discovery_research_for_external_info
cases.prompt:
Research the latest Wayland compositors, compare their features, and recommend
one for a tiling-first power-user setup on NixOS. I need current information,
not stale documentation.

samples.output:
**I recommend Niri for a new tiling-first NixOS setup**, assuming you’re open to scrolling columns. Choose **Sway** instead if you want i3-style nested splits and predictable manual control over every window.

I checked current upstream releases and NixOS package/module sources on **9 November 2026**, distinguishing released features from development documentation.

| Compositor | Current verified release | Workflow and strengths | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Niri** | **26.04 — 25 April 2026** | Scrolling columns; opening windows preserves existing window sizes. Independent workspaces per monitor, tabs, floating windows, overview, gestures, mixed-DPI support and window screencasting. | Its column model is an opinionated workflow; it doesn’t replace arbitrary nested split trees. [Release](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri/releases/tag/v26.04), [features](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri) |
| **Sway** | **1.12 — 25 May 2026** | i3-compatible tiling, explicit layout control and established scripting through IPC. This release adds individual-window capture, color-management protocols and HDR10 with the Vulkan renderer. | My choice for a conventional, restrained workstation; less focused on animated desktop effects. [Project](https://github.com/swaywm/sway), [release](https://github.com/swaywm/sway/releases/tag/1.12) |
| **Hyprland** | **0.57.1 — 3 November 2026** | Dwindle, master, scrolling and monocle layouts; Lua scripting and custom layouts; extensive effects and ecosystem tools. | Broad flexibility comes with configuration maintenance: 0.57 removed legacy `.conf` support. [Layouts](https://wiki.hypr.land/0.57.0/configuring/layouts/), [release](https://github.com/hyprwm/Hyprland/releases/tag/v0.57.1), [migration notice](https://hypr.land/news/update57/) |
| **Mango / MangoWC** | **0.18.5 — 4 November 2026** | dwl-derived, tag-based workflow with scrolling, master-stack, dwindle and grid layouts; scratchpads, overview, IPC, blur and animations. | A compelling alternative for dwm-style users. I’d treat its younger ecosystem and frequent changes as reasons to trial it before committing. [Features](https://github.com/mangowm/mango), [release](https://github.com/mangowm/mango/releases/tag/0.18.5) |
| **River** | **Current 0.4 architecture verified; latest patch unconfirmed** | Separates the compositor from a selectable window-manager process, which can be swapped without restarting applications. | You must choose and integrate the window manager too. Best suited to someone who wants to build their own window-management policy. [Upstream mirror](https://github.com/riverwm/river) |

Three changes make older comparisons particularly misleading:

- **Niri now has mainline blur**, released in 26.04. It also automatically launches **xwayland-satellite** for X11 applications when that dependency is installed; descriptions implying manual X11 setup are outdated. [26.04 release](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri/releases/tag/v26.04), [Xwayland integration](https://niri-wm.github.io/niri/Xwayland.html)
- **Hyprland has built-in scrolling tiling**, alongside Lua-defined custom layouts. Recommending it solely as a dwindle/master compositor misses its current capabilities. Its 0.57 release also adds workspace-specific screen sharing. [Versioned layout documentation](https://wiki.hypr.land/0.57.0/configuring/layouts/), [0.57 announcement](https://hypr.land/news/update57/)
- **Modern River isn’t the old dynamic tiler.** That implementation continues as **river-classic**; current River delegates window-management policy to another process. [Project explanation](https://github.com/riverwm/river)

For NixOS, Niri’s integration makes the recommendation stronger. **Both `nixos-26.05` and `nixos-unstable` currently package 26.04**, so the stable branch already supplies the latest verified release. Its built-in `programs.niri.enable` module wires up the session, systemd units and GNOME portal backend used for screencasting. [Stable package](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/by-name/ni/niri/package.nix), [unstable package](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-unstable/pkgs/by-name/ni/niri/package.nix), [NixOS module](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/nixos/modules/programs/wayland/niri.nix)

My suggested setup is **released Niri, xwayland-satellite, Waybar, Fuzzel and Mako**, with configuration managed declaratively. The optional community **niri-flake** adds structured Nix configuration and build-time validation; it isn’t required to install Niri. [niri-flake documentation](https://github.com/sodiboo/niri-flake)

The deciding question is layout preference: **Niri for stable-width scrolling columns; Sway for deliberate split trees; Hyprland for extensive programmable behavior and effects.** Given your stated priorities, I’d start with Niri.

**I recommend niri for a new tiling-first NixOS setup**, assuming you’re comfortable with scrolling columns. Choose **Sway** instead if you want an i3-style split tree and explicit control over nested layouts.

I checked upstream releases and current module sources on **November 9, 2026**. These are upstream versions; your pinned Nixpkgs revision may provide different ones.

| Compositor | Latest stable verified | Features that matter | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| **niri** | [26.04 — April 25, 2026](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri/releases/tag/v26.04) | Scrolling columns; independent workspaces per monitor; mixed DPI and fractional scaling; floating windows, tabs, overview, gestures and blur. | Its layout model is opinionated: adding windows extends the strip rather than subdividing the screen. |
| **Sway** | [1.12 — May 25, 2026](https://github.com/swaywm/sway/releases/tag/1.12) | i3-compatible tiling, scripting and configuration. Version 1.12 adds individual-window capture, color-management protocols and HDR10 with the Vulkan renderer. | Best suited to deliberate split-tree management; visual effects and layout experimentation are less central. |
| **Hyprland** | [0.57.1 — November 3, 2026](https://github.com/hyprwm/Hyprland/releases/tag/v0.57.1) | Dwindle, master, scrolling and monocle layouts; Lua scripting; extensive effects, rules, IPC and plugins. | More configuration and dependency coordination during upgrades. |
| **river** | [0.5.0 — October 10, 2026](https://codeberg.org/river/river/releases) | Separates rendering from window-management policy; supports interchangeable external window managers. | You must select and integrate a compatible WM before you have a complete tiling workflow. |
| **MangoWC** | [0.18.5 — November 4, 2026](https://github.com/mangowm/mango/releases/tag/0.18.5) | dwl-derived, tag-based workflow; scrolling, master-stack, monocle and other layouts; swallowing, scratchpads, overview and effects. | A younger project with recent configuration changes warrants more evaluation before committing your daily workstation. |

Feature references: [niri](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri), [Sway](https://github.com/swaywm/sway), [Hyprland layouts and configuration](https://wiki.hypr.land/), [river architecture](https://github.com/riverwm/river), [MangoWC](https://github.com/mangowm/mango). The tradeoff assessments are my synthesis.

**Why niri gets my vote:** terminals, editors and browsers keep their useful widths when you open another window. Independent monitor workspaces and workspace restoration after reconnecting displays also suit a laptop-and-dock workflow. You get an overview and modern display handling without assembling a custom layout system. [Upstream design and features](https://github.com/niri-wm/niri).

For NixOS, I’d use this approach:

- Enable **`programs.niri.enable = true;`** at the system level. The current NixOS module supplies session integration and the GNOME portal used for screen sharing. [NixOS module source](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-unstable/nixos/modules/programs/wayland/niri.nix).
- Manage configuration through **current Home Manager’s `wayland.windowManager.niri`**. It supports structured settings, extra KDL and build-time configuration validation. A separate niri flake is therefore optional; check that your pinned Home Manager branch contains this module. [Home Manager source](https://github.com/nix-community/home-manager/blob/master/modules/services/window-managers/niri.nix).
- Include **xwayland-satellite** for legacy applications. Since niri 25.08, integration starts it automatically on demand. Applications that depend on positioning X11 windows at fixed screen coordinates remain an exception. [Xwayland documentation](https://niri-wm.github.io/niri/Xwayland.html).

A few recent changes materially affect the alternatives:

- **Hyprland now has built-in scrolling tiling.** Comparing it with niri solely as “traditional tiling versus scrolling” is outdated. It also introduced Lua configuration in 0.55; older Hyprlang examples need careful checking. Keep compositor, portal and plugin revisions aligned on NixOS. [Layout updates](https://hypr.land/news/update56/), [Lua migration](https://hypr.land/news/26_lua/), [Nix integration guidance](https://wiki.hypr.land/nix/configuring-hyprland-with-home-manager/).
- **Modern river differs substantially from old river tutorials.** Upstream directs users seeking its former integrated dynamic-tiling workflow to **river-classic**. [Current upstream README](https://github.com/riverwm/river).
- **Sway’s HDR situation has changed:** 1.12 explicitly supports HDR10 through Vulkan. If HDR is essential, that deserves a hardware trial before choosing niri. [Release notes](https://github.com/swaywm/sway/releases/tag/1.12).

My choice would change to **Sway for nested split layouts**, **Hyprland for programmable layouts and extensive visual customization**, or **MangoWC for a dwm-style tag workflow**. For a fresh keyboard-driven productivity setup with scrolling tiling, I’d start with **niri**.
